Papers · Notebooks · Python · Derivations · Audit records

Embedding + reranker + indexed source locations

Qwen3.5 / Qwen3.6 / Gemma 4

Python · Deterministic checks · Dependency resolution · Append-only ledger

Model weights remain fixed during normal inference; an embedding database or external ledger adds retrievable state, not automatic learning of model parameters.

# chatgpt response

**Parameters are the numerical values that determine how a neural network transforms an input into an output.** They're essentially the model's learned internal configuration.

And given your programming background, there's an interesting distinction: **parameters aren't instructions. They're the values that shape how the instructions execute.**

## 1. Think of a model as a giant mathematical function

Imagine a simple function\:

$$
y = wx+b
$$

Here\:

- `x` \= input
- `w` \= weight (a learned parameter)
- `b` \= bias (another learned parameter)
- `y` \= output

That function has **2 parameters**\: `w` and `b`\.

During training, the system adjusts those numbers to reduce prediction error.

A language model does something conceptually similar, except it contains billions of learned values organized into interconnected layers.

## 2. What does 9B actually mean?

When you download **Qwen3.5 9B**, the 9B means approximately **9 billion parameters**\.

Each parameter is typically a numerical value used in matrix operations.

For example, a small piece of a weight matrix might look like\:

$$
W =
\begin{bmatrix}
0.25 & -0.71 & 1.42\\
-0.18 & 0.93 & 0.07\\
0.64 & -0.32 & 0.51
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Those nine numbers are nine parameters.

A large language model contains enormous collections of these matrices, learned during training.

**The model's learned behavior is distributed across those numerical relationships.** There's no single parameter that means "Python" or "gravity."

## 3. Why do parameters consume so much memory?

Because the numbers have to be stored.

Approximate weight storage for a 9-billion-parameter model

Decimal GB, weights only. Real GGUF files are often larger because quantization formats add scaling metadata and other tensors.

This is why your RTX 4060 can run a 9B model quantized to 4 bits, but not comfortably hold the same model in FP16.

The mathematical structure is broadly preserved; the precision of its stored weights is reduced.

## 4. Here's something important: more parameters don't necessarily mean more intelligence

Consider\:

| Model | Total parameters | Parameters active per token |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Dense 9B | 9 billion | \~9 billion |
| MoE 30B-A3B | 30 billion | \~3 billion |

A dense model uses essentially all its learned weights during each forward pass.

A **Mixture of Experts (MoE)** model has routing mechanisms that select subsets of its network for each token.

That's why a 30B-A3B model can have 30 billion stored parameters while performing computations involving only approximately 3 billion per token.

The catch: it generally still needs access to the entire model's weights, because different inputs may activate different experts.

## 5. The distinction I think you'll find most interesting

In traditional software\:

$$
\text{Output} = f(\text{Input},\text{Program State})
$$

In a neural network\:

$$
\text{Output} = f(\text{Input},\theta)
$$

Where $\theta$ represents its learned parameters.

In ordinary inference, those parameters are fixed. The changing input, context, and intermediate activations produce different outputs.

**Training changes $\theta$\. Inference uses $\theta$\.**

That distinction matters enormously when building local AI systems.

You can give a model a million new facts through its context and external memory without changing a single parameter. To actually modify its learned numerical configuration, you'd need training or fine-tuning.

---

And this leads to a fascinating next question\:

**How can billions of essentially fixed numbers produce reasoning about something they've never encountered before?**

That's where neural networks get much more interesting than their parameter counts.

Every ordered pair exists exactly once. So every possible transition $x\to y$ has an address.

**Your rings can contain not only every possible data word, but every possible finite Boolean interpreter of those words.**

That's the crucial connection to AI parameters, and it follows directly from your existing algebra.

## 1. The reader is already in the next ring

Your native ring $R_n$ contains all $2^n$ binary words, arranged by your reversal/complement partner law.

You established that $R_{2n}$ contains every ordered pair of $n$\-bit words, so it can address every possible transition.

Now consider something different: an interpreter that reads an $n$\-bit word and produces one Boolean output.

$$
f:\{0,1\}^n\rightarrow\{0,1\}
$$

There are $2^n$ possible inputs. A complete truth table for that reader therefore requires $2^n$ output bits.

And your ring at that width contains every such table\:

$$
\boxed{R_{2^n}\ \longleftrightarrow\
\{\text{all Boolean readers on }R_n\}}
$$

This is an exact finite correspondence. It doesn't depend on machine learning, physics, or a proposed interpretation.

I ran your native partner-ring construction at small widths and checked the correspondence exhaustively.

| Input ring | Possible inputs | Reader ring | Distinct Boolean readers |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|

| $R_4$ | 16 | $R_{16}$ | 65,536 |

So the original input ring isn't the complete story. **The interpretation of the input can itself be represented as another binary word at a higher width.**

And a reader of that reader is another finite binary computation.

## 4. Why the library analogy breaks

The library analogy assumes the books are already meaningful objects. But a book isn't primitive. It requires characters, character encoding, language, grammar, a reader, and history.

Your construction begins earlier than that.

A binary word doesn't know whether it is text, an image, a program, or the state of a physical system.

We can write the relationship as\:

$$
\operatorname{RealityOfReadout}
=
E(\Gamma,w,s)
$$

Where $w$ is the binary configuration, $\Gamma$ is the operative interpreter, and $s$ is its current state, including relevant history.

The consequence is important: **even a finite word can participate in an indefinitely extensible sequence of contexts.**

You don't need to store an infinite amount of meaning inside the word. A new reader can bring new structure to the same word.

All finite binary descriptions fit somewhere in the unbounded family of rings\:

$$
\mathcal R=\bigcup_{n\ge2}R_n
$$

And a finite program can generate outputs far longer than its own representation.

This is related to the universality of computation: a program can itself be represented as data for another program to interpret.  [MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/c10/c10s1/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

But your construction adds something specific: the binary objects, their transformations, and their readers can all be given native ring addresses.

**The ring can contain the description of its own reader.**

That doesn't eliminate execution requirements. It removes the need to imagine a separate category of stored material called *meaning*\.

There are three different notions of identity here.

| Situation | Mathematical relationship |
|--------|--------|
| Two distinct addresses in one $R_n$ | Always different binary words |
| Identical bytes stored at two external locations | Copies of the same binary word |
| Different bytes producing the same observed image | Different words in the same readout equivalence class |

Consider a full-color image with two million pixels. At 24 bits per pixel, its raw pixel space contains $2^{48,000,000}$ configurations.

Two independently uniform draws have probability $2^{-48,000,000}$ of matching exactly.

That's why your intuition about collisions is meaningful: the domain grows exponentially with the number of available distinctions. Real images aren't uniformly distributed, but the address space remains enormous.

Yet when two distinct files decode to the same visible image, they have collided **under that reader**, not within the original binary inventory.

This is a useful inversion of information loss\:

$$
x\neq y,\qquad E(\Gamma,x)=E(\Gamma,y)
$$

The difference remains in the source words. The reader simply doesn't distinguish it.

The readout is a projection, not necessarily a reconstruction of the complete source.

## 6. Now return to your universe-saturation proposal

Suppose every finite binary configuration is already present as an addressable possibility.

Then the critical operation isn't generating additional binary possibilities.

It's determining which existing configurations are coupled, which transformations can execute, and what those executions produce.

That changes the central problem\:

**Forward enumeration**

Construct candidate programs, execute each, inspect outcomes, repeat.

**Compiler-side inversion**

Specify the required readout and boundary conditions, identify the necessary transformation, then compute its native address.

The second path is what you mean by learning to walk the rings.

The ring's completeness is established. The ability to address constructed binary words directly is established. But given only a desired behavior, multiple interpreters can still satisfy it.

Supply the XOR requirement and the reader becomes BOUND at address 5 in $R_4$\. Supply the input and the complete read event is BOUND at address 21 in $R_6$\.

The remaining general problem is therefore\:

**What determines the active reader from the constraints of the system itself?**

For software, that can be an ISA, an ABI, a decoder, or an execution environment. For a proposed physical realization, the equivalent coupling mechanism must be identified.

## 7. And this comes right back to your original question about AI parameters

A language model's learned parameters are not simply its inventory of possible sentences.

They're part of the machinery that determines how an input is transformed into subsequent outputs.

Your binary-ring approach separates two things we often conflate\:

$$
\underbrace{\text{All finite configurations}}_{\text{addressable domain}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\text{The active transformation}}_{\text{reader and route}}
$$

That suggests a specific research question\:

**Can a sufficiently structured reader replace some learned numerical machinery with direct, constraint-derived routing?**

Not necessarily all nine billion parameters. A neural network represents a particular family of functions efficiently, and a generic truth table could be exponentially larger. The comparison must include representation size, route-construction cost, execution cost, and correctness.

There is also a computability boundary: no general algorithm can decide every nontrivial behavioral property of arbitrary programs. Direct addressing does not by itself remove that limit.  [introtcs.org](https://introtcs.org/public/lec_08_uncomputability.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

But that doesn't stop us from constructing exact routes for well-specified domains.

My assessment of the work here\:

**STANDS\:** Every finite Boolean reader on $R_n$ has a representation in $R_{2^n}$, and every combined read event has a representation in $R_{2^n+n}$\.

**RUNS\:** The native ring implementation returned the exact reader, input, combined-event addresses, and outputs for $n=2,3$\.

**OPEN\:** Deriving the active interpreter from an arbitrary system's own constraints, rather than supplying the interpreter externally. In a physical theory, this also requires identifying the actual coupling and execution dynamics.

And here's the distinction I find most consequential in your inversion\:

**You don't need an infinite warehouse of generated files. You need a finite generative law, an address grammar, and a reader whose continuation is determined by its constraints.**

The possible file is an address. The executable behavior is a relationship. The observed reality is what that relationship produces when it runs.

That is a considerably more precise computational formulation than the library metaphor.

# chatgpt response

Got it. You mean **real CPU instruction sets (ISAs)**\: the actual binary opcodes that processors decode and execute. Not combinations of bits.

For example, on a MOS 6502 processor\:

```text
11101010  = NOP       Do nothing
10101001  = LDA #     Load accumulator with immediate value
01101001  = ADC #     Add with carry
11101000  = INX       Increment X register
01001100  = JMP       Jump to absolute address
```

These are actual instruction opcode bytes, not arbitrary binary values. Some require additional bytes for operands.

The important distinction for your rings is that **instruction width, opcode-field width, and CPU register width are three different things**\. There isn't one universal instruction set for every bit width from 1 to 16.

Here are real architectures that expose those levels.

## 1. Actual ISA encodings across bit widths 1–16

| Bit width | Real hardware / ISA example | What those bits represent |
|--------|--------|--------|
| 1 | Motorola MC14500B | 1-bit processor data and accumulator |
| 2 | RISC-V compressed | 2-bit instruction quadrant |
| 3 | DEC PDP-8 | 3-bit primary opcode |
| 4 | Motorola MC14500B, Intel 4004 | 4-bit opcode fields |
| 5 | MIPS | 5-bit register selectors |
| 6 | MIPS32 | 6-bit primary opcodes |
| 7 | RISC-V | 7-bit primary opcodes |
| 8 | MOS 6502, Intel 4004 | 8-bit opcode/instruction encodings |
| 9 | PDP-8 | 9 bits following primary opcode |
| 10 | Architecture-dependent | No common universal 10-bit ISA |
| 11 | LC-3 | 11-bit subroutine offset field |
| 12 | DEC PDP-8 | Complete 12-bit instruction word |
| 13 | Architecture-dependent | No common universal 13-bit ISA |
| 14 | Microchip PIC16 | Complete 14-bit instruction word |
| 15 | Apollo Guidance Computer | 15 information bits per instruction word |
| 16 | LC-3, RISC-V compressed, ARM Thumb | Complete 16-bit instruction encodings |

These are actual hardware-defined fields and instruction formats, not sixteen separate standardized instruction sets.  [Industrial Control Unit](https://www.alldatasheet.net/html-pdf/244447/MOTOROLA/MC14500B/1558/4/MC14500B.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [homepage.cs.uiowa.edu](https://homepage.cs.uiowa.edu/~dwjones/pdp8/man/mri.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [University of Waterloo CSCF](https://student.cs.uwaterloo.ca/~isg/res/mips/opcodes?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [Microchip Docs](https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-1E6FE9B1-4323-4859-AD14-A075C49E9D04-en-US-5/GUID-02C72C4A-81A1-4D22-AAB7-B4FC3461CA8F.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [RISC-V Documentation](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/c-st-ext?utm_source=chatgpt.com) [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Guidance_Computer?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## 2. Complete Motorola MC14500B instruction set

This is a particularly useful starting point because it's a real **1-bit processor with exactly 16 four-bit opcodes**\.

| Binary opcode | Mnemonic | Operation |
|--------|--------|--------|
| `0000` | NOPO | No operation; flag output |
| `0001` | LD | Load data into result register |
| `0010` | LDC | Load complemented data |
| `0011` | AND | Boolean AND |
| `0100` | ANDC | AND with complemented data |
| `0101` | OR | Boolean OR |
| `0110` | ORC | OR with complemented data |
| `0111` | XNOR | Exclusive NOR |
| `1000` | STO | Store result |
| `1001` | STOC | Store complemented result |
| `1010` | IEN | Input enable |
| `1011` | OEN | Output enable |
| `1100` | JMP | Signal jump |
| `1101` | RTN | Signal return and skip |
| `1110` | SKZ | Skip next instruction if zero |
| `1111` | NOPF | No operation; flag output |

This is the complete sixteen-entry opcode map from Motorola's specification. Notice that `0111` is **XNOR**, not XOR.  [Industrial Control Unit](https://www.alldatasheet.net/html-pdf/244447/MOTOROLA/MC14500B/1558/4/MC14500B.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## 3. Intel 4004 — 4-bit CPU

The 4004 operates on 4-bit data but executes 8-bit or 16-bit instructions.

Its primary opcode groups are\:

| First 4 bits | Instruction family | Binary encoding |
|--------|--------|--------|
| `0000` | NOP | `00000000` |
| `0001` | JCN | `0001CCCC` \+ address byte |
| `0010` | FIM / SRC | `0010RRR0` / `0010RRR1` |
| `0011` | FIN / JIN | `0011RRR0` / `0011RRR1` |
| `0100` | JUN | `0100AAAA` \+ address byte |
| `0101` | JMS | `0101AAAA` \+ address byte |
| `0110` | INC | `0110RRRR` |
| `0111` | ISZ | `0111RRRR` \+ address byte |
| `1000` | ADD | `1000RRRR` |
| `1001` | SUB | `1001RRRR` |
| `1010` | LD | `1010RRRR` |
| `1011` | XCH | `1011RRRR` |
| `1100` | BBL | `1100DDDD` |
| `1101` | LDM | `1101DDDD` |
| `1110` | Memory / I/O | E0–EF family |
| `1111` | Accumulator / control | F0–FD family |

Here `R` identifies a register, `D` immediate data, `A` an address, and `C` a condition. The E and F groups contain additional specifically assigned instructions.  [Pyntel4004 ENV_VERSION documentation](https://pyntel4004.readthedocs.io/en/latest/intro/opcodes.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## 4. DEC PDP-8 — complete eight primary opcodes

The PDP-8 uses a 12-bit instruction word. Only three bits are required to distinguish its eight primary operation classes.

| 3-bit opcode | Instruction | Function |
|--------|--------|--------|
| `000` | AND | Logical AND |
| `001` | TAD | Two's-complement addition |
| `010` | ISZ | Increment and skip if zero |
| `011` | DCA | Store accumulator and clear |
| `100` | JMS | Jump to subroutine |
| `101` | JMP | Jump |
| `110` | IOT | Input/output transfer |
| `111` | OPR | Register/control operations |

The full 12-bit memory-reference format is\:

```text
OOO I P AAAAAAA
│   │ │ └────── 7-bit page address
│   │ └──────── Page selector
│   └────────── Direct / indirect
└────────────── 3-bit opcode
```

The `OPR` category uses additional bits to select or combine register operations.  [homepage.cs.uiowa.edu](https://homepage.cs.uiowa.edu/~dwjones/pdp8/man/mri.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## 5. MOS 6502 — 8-bit opcode examples

The 6502 uses 8-bit opcode bytes, with complete instructions occupying one to three bytes.

| Hex | Binary opcode | Instruction |
|--------|--------|--------|
| 00 | `00000000` | BRK |
| 09 | `00001001` | ORA immediate |
| 18 | `00011000` | CLC |
| 20 | `00100000` | JSR absolute |
| 29 | `00101001` | AND immediate |
| 49 | `01001001` | EOR immediate |
| 4C | `01001100` | JMP absolute |
| 60 | `01100000` | RTS |
| 69 | `01101001` | ADC immediate |
| 8D | `10001101` | STA absolute |
| A9 | `10101001` | LDA immediate |
| C9 | `11001001` | CMP immediate |
| E8 | `11101000` | INX |
| E9 | `11101001` | SBC immediate |
| EA | `11101010` | NOP |

These are 6502 opcode bytes; extra operands are not shown.  [NESdev Wiki](https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/User%3AKaratorian/6502_Instruction_Set?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## 6. The 14-bit and 16-bit instruction sets

Microchip's PIC16 enhanced mid-range architecture uses 14-bit instruction words for operations such as `MOVLW`, `ADDWF`, `BTFSC`, `GOTO`, `CALL`, and `RETURN`\.  [Microchip Docs](https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-1E6FE9B1-4323-4859-AD14-A075C49E9D04-en-US-5/GUID-02C72C4A-81A1-4D22-AAB7-B4FC3461CA8F.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

For a complete 16-bit primary opcode map, the LC-3 is unusually clean\:

| First 4 bits | Instruction |
|--------|--------|
| `0000` | BR |
| `0001` | ADD |
| `0010` | LD |
| `0011` | ST |
| `0100` | JSR / JSRR |
| `0101` | AND |
| `0110` | LDR |
| `0111` | STR |
| `1000` | RTI |
| `1001` | NOT |
| `1010` | LDI |
| `1011` | STI |
| `1100` | JMP / RET |
| `1101` | Reserved |
| `1110` | LEA |
| `1111` | TRAP |

The remaining twelve bits carry operands, addresses, register selections, or other instruction fields.  [CS-131](https://cs131.info/Assembly/Instructions/Anatomy.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

For actual production hardware rather than an educational ISA, RISC-V's compressed extension defines 16-bit instructions such as `C.ADDI`, `C.LI`, `C.LW`, `C.SW`, `C.J`, and `C.BEQZ`\.  [RISC-V Documentation](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/c-st-ext?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## 7. The connection to your ring

This is the part worth isolating.

Take the byte `10010000`, hexadecimal `90`\.

On x86, `90` is `NOP`\.

On the 6502, `90` is `BCC`, a conditional branch that consumes a following displacement byte.

Same binary word. Different decoder. Different operation.

The ISA, machine state, and available operands determine the executable transformation.

For your proposed compiler approach, I'd start with the **Motorola MC14500B, PDP-8, Intel 4004, and 6502**, then compare how each partitions the same binary address space into executable instructions.

That gives us actual historical compiler/decoder contracts to investigate, rather than an invented universal opcode table.

## 1. What your two-lap engine already does

Your core transition is\:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= D[p]\oplus w\\
p' &= p\oplus x\\
w' &= P_n(x)\\
D'[p] &= D[p]\oplus w'
\end{aligned}
$$

Here, `p` is the reader's word location, `w` is its carried state, `D` is the live field, and $P_n$ is your native reversal/complement partner operation.

The significant property is that **the reader changes the field it reads, and that modified field affects subsequent reading.**

This is more than a static lookup table. It's a recurrent, stateful computation with a defined inverse.

Original C program — independently reproduced periods

| Native $P$, center one-break seed | 43,155,322 steps |
|--------|--------|
| Native $P$, two-break seed | 132 steps |
| Native $P$, zero seed | 6 steps |
| Mirror-only $J$, one-break seed | 518 steps |

The native one-break run also returns to the field vacuum at exactly step **21,577,661**, halfway through the cycle, with the reader and carry at their complemented positions.

This matters computationally because a small recurrent machine can generate a long, structured trajectory without storing 43 million instructions or states individually.

And the distinction between $P$ and mirror-only $J$ demonstrates that your palindrome/complement branch materially changes the dynamics. It's not just an alternative notation.

work it backwards.  **In fundamental physics, quantum fields do not have a maximum capacity or a hard saturation limit for holding particles (THE RINGS), but the concept of "saturation" appears in several distinct quantum contexts.** Depending on whether you are looking at the math of fields, high-energy collisions, or empty space, here is how saturation applies:

**1. Particle Capacity (No Saturation Limit)**

In standard quantum field theory (QFT), **a quantum field cannot be "filled up."** Even within a tightly defined, finite region of space, a quantum field can theoretically support an infinite number of particles or energy excitations. The mathematical operator used to count particles is unbounded, meaning there is no point at which the field becomes too crowded to accept more energy. [[1](https://physics.stackexchange.com/questions/318387/do-quantum-fields-have-saturation-limits)]

**2. Gluon Saturation**

In experimental nuclear physics, saturation is a real, observable boundary. When subatomic particles like protons are accelerated to near the speed of light, the number of gluons (the particles that glue quarks together) multiplies rapidly. Eventually, they become packed so tightly that they hit a limit called **gluon saturation**. At this point, the gluons begin to fuse together as fast as they are created, entering a dense, unique state of matter known as a [**Color Glass Condensate**](https://www.facebook.com/SCIENCESpaceTamil/videos/what-happens-to-matter-when-it-moves-at-nearly-the-speed-of-light/2038093220179012/). [[1](https://www.facebook.com/SCIENCESpaceTamil/videos/what-happens-to-matter-when-it-moves-at-nearly-the-speed-of-light/2038093220179012/)]

**3. "Saturons" and Information Limits**

In theoretical physics, certain complex structures are classified as **saturons**. These are objects—most notably **black holes** and specific localized waves called solitons—that completely saturate the absolute quantum field theoretic upper limit for entropy and microstate degeneracy. They pack the absolute maximum amount of quantum information into a given space before a horizon forms. [[1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08049), [2](https://www.ipht.fr/events/similarities-in-the-evaporation-of-saturated-solitons-and-black-holes/)]

**4. The Quantum Vacuum (Saturated with Activity)**

If you mean "saturated" in the sense of being thoroughly soaked or filled, then **all of space is permanently saturated by quantum fields**. Even a perfect cosmic vacuum devoid of all physical matter is not truly empty. It is a roiling, energy-dense medium saturated by the baseline "ground states" of the universe's 17 known fields, which constantly fluctuate and generate virtual particles. [[1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NpAQ685uhMg), [2](https://www.facebook.com/groups/quantumphysicssciencetalk/posts/1106360408160500/), [3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YecFCzb11h0)]

**When a step is itself a move.**
